Surah al-Mu'minun

Makkiyyah (Meccan)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Salihi related to us; Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Hiri related to us; Hajib ibn Ahmad al-Tusi related to us; Muhammad ibn Hammad related to us; Abd al-Razzaq related to us; Yunus ibn Sulayman related to us: Yunus, the companion of Ayla, dictated to me, from Ibn Shihab, from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd al-Qari, who said: I heard Umar ibn al-Khattab say: "When revelation came down upon the Prophet (ﷺ), a sound like the buzzing of bees could be heard near his face. So we waited for a while" — and in another narration: "One day revelation came down upon us, and we waited for a while" — "then he faced the qiblah, raised his hands and said: 'O Allah, increase us and do not diminish us; honour us and do not humiliate us; give us and do not deprive us; prefer us and do not prefer others over us; and be pleased with us.' Then he said: 'Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise.'" Then he recited: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ up to ten verses.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ali ibn al-Madini, and a group [of narrators] also related it from Abd al-Razzaq, and they said: "Give us and do not deprive us, and make us content and be pleased with us."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in Tafsir, chapter: "And from Surat al-Mu'minun" (9/16-17); Imam Ahmad (1/34); al-Hakim authenticated it and al-Dhahabi agreed (1/535); and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah (5/177), who said: "This is a hasan hadith. Yunus, the companion of Ayla, is Yunus ibn Yazid al-Ayli, the companion of al-Zuhri."]]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾. "Qad" (certainly) is a particle of emphasis. The muhaqqiqun (verifying scholars) said: "Qad" brings the past close to the present, indicating that success has already been attained by them and that they are in that state now, and this is more emphatic than stating the verb alone. "Al-falah" (success) means deliverance and endurance. Ibn Abbas said: "Those who affirmed the Oneness [of Allah] have been made happy and remain in Paradise."

﴿Who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾. The scholars differed over the meaning of khushu'. Ibn Abbas said: "mukhbitun" (humble, lowly). Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "khaifun" (fearful). Muqatil said: "mutawadi'un" (humble). Mujahid said: it is lowering the gaze and lowering the voice.

Khushu' is close in meaning to khudu' (submission), except that khudu' is in the body, whereas khushu' is in the heart, the body, the gaze and the voice. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Gracious﴾ [Ta-Ha: 108].

It is related from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that it means not turning right or left. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it means not recognising who is on one's right or left, and not turning [one's attention] away, out of khushu' to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Abd al-Wahid al-Malihi related to us; Ahmad al-Nu'aymi related to us; Muhammad ibn Yusuf related to us; Muhammad ibn Isma'il related to us: Musaddad related to us; Abu al-Ahwas related to us; Ashath ibn Salim related to us, from his father, from Masruq, from Aisha, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about turning [the head] during prayer, and he said: "It is a snatching which Satan snatches from the prayer of the servant."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Adhan, chapter: Turning in prayer (2/234); and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah (3/251).]]

Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi related to us; Abu Ali Zahir ibn Ahmad related to us; Abu al-Hasan al-Qasim ibn Bakr al-Tayalisi in Baghdad related to us; Abu Umayyah Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Tarsusi related to us; Abd al-Ghaffar ibn Ubayd Allah related to us; Salih ibn Abi al-Akhdar related to us, from al-Zuhri, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abu Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah continues to turn towards the servant as long as he is in his prayer, so long as he does not turn; but if he turns, He turns away from him."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud in al-Salah, chapter: Turning in prayer (1/429); al-Nasa'i in al-Sahw, chapter: Severity regarding turning in prayer (3/8); Ibn Khuzaymah in his Sahih (1/244); Imam Ahmad (5/172); al-Hakim (1/236), who said: "This hadith has a sound chain but they did not record it, and this Abu al-Ahwas is a client of the Banu al-Layth, a Successor from the people of Madinah, whom al-Zuhri deemed trustworthy and narrated from; and there was a debate between him and Sa'd ibn Ibrahim about its meaning." And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah (3/252), who said: "Salih ibn Abi al-Akhdar is weak; he narrates from al-Zuhri." This hadith was also related by Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak and others from Yunus from al-Zuhri. Al-Mundhiri said: "This Abu al-Ahwas is not known by name; he is a client of the Banu Layth, and it was said he was a client of the Banu Ghifar. al-Zuhri did not narrate from him. Yahya ibn Ma'in said: 'He is nothing.' Abu Ahmad al-Karabisi said: 'He is not reliable according to them.'" Mukhtasar Sunan Abi Dawud (1/429); al-Nawawi in al-Khulasah said: "It contains obscurity, but Abu Dawud did not declare it weak, so it is hasan in his view." See Nasb al-Rayah (2/89).]]

Amr ibn Dinar said: it is tranquillity and good bearing. Ibn Sirin and others said: it is that you do not raise your gaze from the place of your prostration.

Abu Hurayrah said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to raise their gaze to the sky during prayer, but when this was revealed — ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ — they cast their gaze to the places of prostration.

Abd al-Wahid al-Malihi related to us; Ahmad al-Nu'aymi related to us; Muhammad ibn Yusuf related to us; Muhammad ibn Isma'il related to us; Ali ibn Abd Allah related to us; Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us; Ibn Abi Arubah related to us; Qatadah related to us, that Anas ibn Malik narrated to them, saying: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What is the matter with people who raise their gaze to the sky during their prayer?" His words on this were so severe that he said: "They must stop this, or their sight will be snatched away."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Sahw, chapter: Raising the gaze to the sky in prayer (2/233); and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah (3/258).]]

Atha' said: it is that you do not fidget with any part of your body during prayer. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw a man playing with his beard during prayer and said: "If this man's heart were humble, his limbs would be humble too."[[Al-Manawi said in al-Fath al-Samawi (2/854): al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related it in Nawadir al-Usul with a weak chain from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and in it is Sulayman ibn Amr, Abu Dawud al-Nakha'i, one of those accused of fabricating hadith. See also Irwa' al-Ghalil (2/92-93) and Silsilat al-Ahadith al-Da'ifah (1/143-144).]]

Abu Uthman al-Dabbi related to us; Abu Muhammad al-Jirahi related to us; Abu al-Abbas al-Mahbubi related to us; Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi related to us; Sa'id related to us, from Abd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi; Sufyan ibn Uyaynah related to us, from al-Zuhri, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abu Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When any one of you stands for prayer, let him not wipe the pebbles, for mercy faces him."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud in al-Salah, chapter: Wiping pebbles in prayer (1/443); al-Tirmidhi in al-Salah, chapter: What has been related about disliking wiping pebbles in prayer (2/382); al-Nasa'i in al-Sahw, chapter: Prohibition of wiping pebbles in prayer (3/6); Ibn Majah in al-Iqamah, chapter: Wiping pebbles, no. (1027) (1/328); Ibn Hibban in al-Mawaqit, chapter: What is forbidden in prayer, p. 131 of Mawarid al-Zaman; Imam Ahmad (5/150); and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah (3/158).]]

It is said: khushu' in prayer is the gathering of one's resolve, turning away from everything else, and reflecting on what passes over one's tongue of recitation and remembrance.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 3–4:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And those who turn away from vain talk﴾. Ata reported from Ibn Abbas: "From polytheism (shirk)." Al-Hasan said: "From sins (ma'asi)." Al-Zajjaj said: "From every falsehood, frivolity, and what is not permissible in speech and action." It was also said: it refers to the disbelievers' responding to them with abuse and insult. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72], meaning: when they hear foul speech, they keep themselves too honorable to engage in it.

﴿And those who are active in giving zakat﴾. That is, those who pay the obligatory zakat. He expressed the paying of it with the word "doing" (fi'l) because it is an act. It was also said: zakat here means righteous deeds, that is, "and those who are active in righteous deeds."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 3–4:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And those who turn away from vain talk﴾. Ata reported from Ibn Abbas: "From polytheism (shirk)." Al-Hasan said: "From sins (ma'asi)." Al-Zajjaj said: "From every falsehood, frivolity, and what is not permissible in speech and action." It was also said: it refers to the disbelievers' responding to them with abuse and insult. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72], meaning: when they hear foul speech, they keep themselves too honorable to engage in it.

﴿And those who are active in giving zakat﴾. That is, those who pay the obligatory zakat. He expressed the paying of it with the word "doing" (fi'l) because it is an act. It was also said: zakat here means righteous deeds, that is, "and those who are active in righteous deeds."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 5–10:

﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ al-Farj (the private part): a term that encompasses the private part of both the man and the woman. Hifz al-farj (guarding the private part) means abstaining from what is forbidden (haram).

﴿Except from their spouses﴾ That is, from among their spouses, and "ʿalā" (on) here carries the meaning of "min" (from).

﴿Or what their right hands possess﴾ "Mā" is in the position of the genitive (majrūr), meaning: or what their right hands possess. The verse refers to men specifically, as evidenced by His saying: "or what their right hands possess," and a woman may not enjoy sexual relations with her male slave.

﴿For they are not blameworthy﴾ That is, one who guards his private part except with his wife or his female slave is not blamed for that. He is blamed only if it is done in a manner the Shariah has permitted; intercourse in other than the permitted place, or during menstruation and postpartum bleeding, is prohibited, and one who does it is blameworthy.

﴿But whoever seeks beyond that﴾ That is, whoever seeks and desires other than wives and owned female slaves, ﴿those are the transgressors﴾: the wrongdoers who exceed the lawful into the unlawful. In this is evidence that masturbation (istimna' bil-yad) is haram, and this is the view of most scholars. Ibn Jurayj said: I asked ʿAtaʾ about it, and he said: It is makruh (disliked). I have heard that some people will be resurrected with their hands pregnant, and I think they are these people. It is narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that he said: Allah punished a nation who used to toy with their male organs.

﴿And those who are faithful to their trusts﴾ Ibn Kathir read "li-amanatihim" in the singular here and in Surat al-Maʿarij, due to His saying: ﴿and their covenant﴾. The rest read it in the plural, like His saying, mighty and majestic: "Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners" [al-Nisa': 58]. ﴿And their covenants they uphold﴾ means: they guard what they have been entrusted with, and the agreements they made with people, and they fulfill their obligations. Trusts vary: some are between Allah the Exalted and the servant, such as prayer, fasting, and the acts of worship that Allah has made obligatory upon him; and some are between servants, such as deposits and commissions. The servant must fulfill all of them.

﴿And those who guard their prayers﴾ Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "salatihim" in the singular, while the others read "salawatihim" in the plural.

﴿Maintain them﴾ That is, they persist in preserving them and observe their times. He repeated the mention of prayer to clarify that maintaining it is obligatory, just as humility (khushu') in it is obligatory.

﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ the people of this description, ﴿who will inherit﴾ the dwellings of the people of the Fire in Paradise.

It is narrated from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but has two dwellings: a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. If he dies and enters the Fire, the people of Paradise inherit his dwelling." [Narrated by Ibn Majah in al-Zuhd, chapter: Description of Paradise: 2/1453, no. 4341, and he said in al-Zawa'id: this chain is sound according to the conditions of al-Bukhari and Muslim.] And this is His saying: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾.

Mujahid said: For each one there is a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. As for the believer, he builds his dwelling which is in Paradise and demolishes his dwelling which is in the Fire; as for the disbeliever, he demolishes his dwelling which is in Paradise and builds his dwelling which is in the Fire.

Some of them said: The meaning of inheritance is that their affair will end in Paradise and they will attain it, just as the matter of an inheritance ends with the heir.

Al-Kalbi said: "from a drop extracted from clay, and the clay is Adam, peace be upon him." It was also said that what is meant by "man" here is Adam. As for His words ﴿from an extract﴾: that is, extracted from every kind of soil.

﴿Then We made him a drop [of semen]﴾: meaning, the one who is man, We made him a drop, ﴿in a firm resting place﴾: secure, which is the womb, made firm [i.e., prepared] for their settling therein until the appointed term.

Qatadah said: the growth of teeth and hair. Ibn Juraij related from Mujahid that it is the attainment of youth. From al-Hasan, he said: male or female. Al-'Awfi related from Ibn 'Abbas that this is the progression of his states after birth: from the first cry to nursing, to sitting, to standing, to walking, to weaning, to eating and drinking, to reaching puberty, and moving about in the lands, and what comes after that.

﴿So blessed is Allah﴾, meaning: He deserves exaltation and praise, in that He has always been and always will be.

﴿the Best of Creators﴾, the best of those who fashion and decree. In the language, "al-khalq" means measuring/decreeing. Mujahid said: they fashion, and Allah fashions, and Allah is the best of fashioners; it is said "rajul khaliq", meaning a craftsman (sani').

Ibn Juraij said: He only used the plural "al-khaliqin" because 'Isa used to create, as He said: "I create for you from clay" [Al 'Imran: 49], so Allah informed about Himself that He is the best of creators [[al-Tabari recorded these two opinions and preferred the view of Mujahid, because the Arabs call every craftsman a creator, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr: "Indeed you measure what you create, and some of the daughters of the people create, then do not measure."

See: Tafsir al-Tabari 18/11; Zad al-Masir 5/463-464.]].

﴿Then indeed you, after that, will surely die﴾. The word "mayyit" with the doubled letter (mayyit) and "ma'it" refers to one who has not yet died but will die, whereas "mayt" with a single letter refers to one who has already died. For this reason, the lightened form is not permissible here, as in His saying: "Indeed you will die and indeed they will die" [al-Zumar: 30].

﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised up﴾.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 17–18:**

﴿And We have certainly created above you seven paths﴾. That is, seven heavens. They were called *taraʾiq* (paths) because they are layered (*tatarruq*), meaning that some of them are above others. It is said: "I layered the sandal" (*tarraqtu al-naʿl*) when I placed one part of it over another. It is also said that they were called *taraʾiq* because they are the paths of the angels.

﴿And We were not unaware of the creation﴾. That is, We were guarding them from the sky falling upon them and destroying them, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ [al-Hajj: 65].

It is also said: "We did not leave them neglected (*sudan*), without command and prohibition."

It is also said: "And We were not unaware of the creation," meaning: We built above them a sky in which We set the sun, the moon and the stars.

﴿And We sent down water from the sky in measure﴾, which Allah knows. Muqatil said: "In the measure that suffices them for their livelihood." ﴿Then We made it settle in the earth﴾, meaning what remains in the pools (*ghudran*) and the stagnant waters (*mustanqaʿat*), from which people benefit in the summer when the rain stops. It is also said: "Then We made it settle in the earth, then We brought forth from it springs." So all the water of the earth comes from the sky. ﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾, so that you would perish of thirst, your livestock would die, and your lands would be ruined.

It is reported in a report: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down four rivers from Paradise: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Euphrates (Furat) and the Tigris (Dijlah)." [[Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/95, from Ibn Abi al-Dunya, from Ibn ʿAttaf.]]

Muqatil ibn Hayyan related from Ikrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down five rivers from Paradise: Jayhun, Sayhun, the Tigris (Dijlah), the Euphrates (Furat) and the Nile (al-Nil). Allah sent them down from one spring of the springs of Paradise, from the lowest level of its levels, upon the wings of Jibril. Allah entrusted them to the mountains and made them flow in the earth, and placed in them benefits for people. This is the meaning of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We sent down water from the sky in measure, then We made it settle in the earth﴾. When the time of the emergence of Gog and Magog comes, Allah sends Jibril, and he lifts from the earth the Qur'an and all knowledge, the Black Stone from the corner of the House, the Station of Ibrahim, the Ark of Musa with what is in it, and these five rivers. All of that is raised up to the sky. This is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾. When these things are lifted from the earth, its people lose the good of religion and of the world." [[Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/95, from Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib, with a weak chain. See also al-Bahr al-Muhit: 6/400.]]

This hadith was also related by the Imam al-Hasan ibn Yusuf, from Uthman ibn Saʿid, by way of *ijazah* (authorized transmission), from Saʿid ibn Sabiq al-Iskandarani, from Maslamah ibn ʿAli, from Muqatil ibn Hayyan. [[Maslamah ibn ʿAli al-Khushani is abandoned (*matruk*). See Ibn Hajar's al-Taqrib.]]

**Al-Baghawi, *Ma'alim al-Tanzil*, commentary on Surah 23, verses 19–20:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We produced for you therewith﴾, meaning: with the water, ﴿gardens of palm trees and grapevines, for you in them﴾, meaning: in the gardens, ﴿are many fruits, and from them you eat﴾, in winter and in summer. The palm trees and grapevines are singled out for mention because they are the most abundant fruits of the Arabs.

﴿And a tree﴾, meaning: And We produced for you a tree ﴿that issues from Mount Sinai﴾, and it is the olive tree. The people of the Hijaz and Abu 'Amr read "Sīnā'" with a kasra on the sīn. The others read it with a fatha on it, and they differed over its meaning and over "Sīnīn" in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and Mount Sinīn﴾ [al-Tin: 2]. Mujahid said: its meaning is blessing, that is, from a blessed mountain. Qatadah said: its meaning is beauty, that is, from the beautiful mountain. al-Dahhak said: it is in Nabatean (the language of the Nabataeans), and its meaning is beauty. 'Ikrimah said: it is in Hebrew (Habashi). al-Kalbi said: its meaning is trees, that is, a mountain with trees. It was said: it is in Syriac, meaning "intertwined with trees." Muqatil said: every mountain in which there are fruit-bearing trees is "Sīnā'," and "Sīnīn" is in the language of the Nabat. It was said: it is fay'āl from al-sanā' (elevation), which is height. Ibn Zayd said: it is the mountain from which Musa (ﷺ) was called, between Egypt and Aylah. Mujahid also said: Sayna' is the name of a specific stone, and the mountain was attributed to it because it is present there. 'Ikrimah said: it is the name of the place in which this mountain lies.

[al-Tabari mentioned these sayings (18/13–14), and he gave his preference, saying: "The correct view on this matter is that Sina' is a name to which al-Tur is attributed, by which it is known, just as it is said 'Jabalay Tayyi'' (the two mountains of Tayy), which are attributed to Tayy. If the matter were as those who said its meaning is 'blessed mountain' or 'beautiful' said, then al-Tur would be indefinite (tanwin), and His saying 'Sina'' would be an adjective of it. Yet Sina' in the sense of 'blessed' or 'beautiful' is not known in the speech of the Arabs, so it would be made an adjective of the mountain. Rather, the correct view, God willing, is what Ibn 'Abbas said: that it is a mountain known by that name, and it is the mountain from which Musa (ﷺ) was called, and it is, together with that, blessed, not that the meaning of Sina' is 'blessed'."]

﴿It grows with the oil﴾. Ibn Kathir, the people of Basra and Ya'qub read "tunbitu" with a damma on the tā' and a kasra on the bā', while the others read it with a fatha on the tā' and a damma on the bā'. Whoever reads it with a fatha on the tā', its meaning is: it grows, it bears the oil, which is the olive. It was said: it grows and the oil is with it. As for whoever reads it with a damma on the tā', they differed about it. Some of them said: the bā' is extra (zā'idah), its meaning being: it causes the oil to grow, as one says "akhadtu thawbahu" and "akhadtu bi-thawbihi" (I took his garment). Others said: nabata and anbata are two dialects with one meaning, as Zuhayr said:

*I saw the people of need around their dwellings,*
*their companions, until, when the herbage grew (anbata al-baql)...*

That is, it grew (nabata). ﴿And a relish for the eaters﴾. The ṣibgh and ṣibbāgh: the condiment that colours the bread when it is dipped into it and takes on its colour. The idām (relish) is everything eaten with bread, whether or not the bread takes on its colour from it. Muqatil said: God placed in this tree a relish (udm) and oil (duhn); the udm is the olive, and the duhn is the oil. He said: the Tur was singled out for the olive because the first olive grew there. It is said that the olive was the first tree to grow in the world after the Flood.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 21–26:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And indeed in the livestock there is a lesson for you﴾, i.e., a sign by which you may take heed. ﴿We give you to drink﴾ — Nafi' recited it with the nun [and its fath-ha (vowel a)]¹, and Abu Ja'far recited it here with the ta' and its fath-ha. ﴿of what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾. ﴿And upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾, i.e., upon the camels on land, and upon the ship at sea.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah"﴾, make Him one (wahhidu-hu), ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾, no worshipped one besides Him, ﴿Will you not then fear Allah?﴾, i.e., will you not fear His punishment if you worship other than Him?

﴿The eminent ones who disbelieved among his people said, "This is not but a man like you who wants to make himself superior over you"﴾, i.e., who seeks to be honoured with superiority over you, so that he becomes one who is followed while you become his followers. ﴿And if Allah had willed﴾ that nothing be worshipped besides Him, ﴿He would have sent down angels﴾, meaning to convey the revelation.

﴿We have not heard of this﴾ which Noah calls us to ﴿among our forefathers of old﴾. It was also said: "We have not heard of this", i.e., of sending a human as a messenger.

﴿He is not but a man in whom there is madness (jinnah)﴾, i.e., insanity (junun), ﴿so wait for him for a time﴾, i.e., until he dies, so that you may be rid of him.

﴿He said, "My Lord, support me, because they have denied me"﴾, i.e., help me by destroying them for their denying me.

---

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 23, verses 27–32:**

﴿So We revealed to him: "Build the ship under Our eyes and by Our revelation. Then when Our command comes and the oven boils over, load into it"﴾: "Enter into it." It is said: "I inserted it (*salaktuhu*) into such-and-such," and "I caused it to enter (*aslaktuhu*) into it." ﴿from every pair two, and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth among them﴾: that is, those against whom the judgment of destruction has already been decreed.

﴿And do not plead with Me concerning those who did wrong; indeed, they are to be drowned﴾. ﴿So when you have settled (*istawayta*), you and those with you, upon the ship, then say: "Praise be to Allah, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people"﴾: that is, "have become upright (*i'tadalta*)." "The wrongdoing people" means the disbelievers.

﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to disembark at a blessed landing place"﴾. Abu Bakr, on the authority of Asim, read *"manzilan"* (مَنْزِلًا) with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *zay*, meaning the place of alighting (*mawdi' al-nuzul*). It has been said that this refers to the ship after boarding, and it has been said that it refers to the earth after disembarking. It is possible that he meant within the ship, and it is possible that he meant after leaving it. The rest of the readers read *"munzalan"* (مُنْزَلًا) with a damma on the *mim* and a fatha on the *zay*, meaning the act of causing to alight (*inzalan*). So the blessing in the ship is deliverance, and the blessing in the disembarking after leaving it is the abundance of offspring from his three sons. ﴿And You are the best of those who cause to alight﴾.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, what I have mentioned of the matter of Nuh, the ship, and the destruction of the enemies of Allah, ﴿are signs﴾, that is, proofs of His power. ﴿And indeed We were ever testing﴾. And it has been said: "And We were not but testing," that is, testing them by sending Nuh, admonishing and reminding them, ﴿to see what they would do﴾ before the punishment descended upon them. [31/b]

﴿Then We produced after them﴾, that is, after their destruction, ﴿another generation﴾. ﴿Then We sent among them a messenger from among themselves﴾, meaning Hud and his people. It has been said: Salih and his people. The first is more apparent. ﴿"Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?"﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 33–42:

﴿And the chiefs of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter said﴾, that is, the return to the Hereafter, ﴿and whom We had given luxury in the life of this world: "This is only a human being like you. He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink"﴾, that is, of what you drink.

﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, then indeed you would be losers﴾, meaning, defrauded.

﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾, meaning, brought forth alive from your graves. He repeated "annakum" (that you) because the speech was long. The meaning of the speech is: "Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?" It is the same in the recitation of Abdullah. Its parallel in the Qur'an is: ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, to abide therein forever?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 63].

﴿Far, far is what you are promised﴾. Ibn Abbas said: it is a word expressing distance, meaning: far is what you are promised. Abu Ja'far recited "hayhatu hayhatin" with a kasra on the ta'. Nasr ibn Asim recited it with a damma. All of these are valid dialects. Whoever reads it with a fatha treats it like "ayna" (where) and "kayfa" (how). Whoever reads it with a damma treats it like "mundhu" (since), "qatt" (ever) and "haythu" (where). Whoever reads it with a kasra treats it like "amsi" (yesterday) and "ha'ulaa'" (these). Most reciters pause on it with a ta' (written as ta'), and it is narrated from al-Kisa'i that he paused on it with a ha' (written as ha').

﴿There is none but our life of this world; we die and we live﴾, meaning, the world. It is said that there is inversion in this, meaning: we live and we die, because they denied resurrection after death. It is also said: the fathers die and the sons live. It is also said: one people die and another people live.

﴿And we are not to be resurrected﴾, meaning, raised up after death.

﴿He is only a man who has invented a lie against Allah, and we are not going to believe him﴾, meaning, we will not affirm the resurrection after death. "He" refers to the Messenger.

﴿He said: "My Lord, help me, because they have denied me."﴾

﴿He said: "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ ﴿So the Blast seized them in truth, and We made them debris. So away with the wrongdoing people!﴾ ﴿Then We produced after them other generations.﴾

﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ meaning: with a clear proof, from the hand and the staff, and other than them.

﴿To Fir'awn and his chiefs, but they acted arrogantly﴾ they magnified themselves against faith, ﴿and they were a haughty people﴾ domineering and tyrannical, subjugating others through oppression.

﴿So they said﴾ meaning Fir'awn and his people, ﴿"Shall we believe in two mortals like us?"﴾ meaning Musa and Harun, ﴿"while their people are servants to us?"﴾ meaning obedient and humbled. The Arabs call anyone who submits to a king "his servant" ('abid).

﴿So they denied them both, and so they became among those destroyed﴾ by drowning.

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book﴾ the Tawrah, ﴿that they might be guided﴾ meaning, so that his people might be guided by it.

﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾ a proof of Our power. He did not say "two signs." It was said: its meaning is that their state is one sign. And it was said: its meaning is that We made each of them a sign, like His saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾ [al-Kahf: 33].

﴿And We sheltered them both on a height﴾ al-Rabwah is the elevated place of the earth. Opinions differ regarding it. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: it is Damascus, and this is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Muqatil. al-Dahhak said: the Ghawtah of Damascus. Abu Hurayrah said: it is al-Ramlah. 'Ata reported from Ibn 'Abbas: it is Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is the view of Qatadah and Ka'b. Ka'b said: it is the nearest of the earth to the sky by eighteen miles. Ibn Zayd said: it is Egypt. al-Suddi said: the land of Palestine. [[Al-Tabari mentioned these opinions (18/25–27), then said, giving preference: "The most preferable of these interpretations is that it is an elevated place, level and with flowing water, and the description of al-Ramlah does not fit, for al-Ramlah has no apparent spring. Allah the Exalted described this rabwah as having a settled place and a spring."]]

﴿Settled, with a spring﴾ meaning: level, flat and wide, upon which its inhabitants settle.

﴿and a spring﴾ al-Ma'in is the flowing, visible water which the eyes see; it is a passive participle from 'anahu, yu'inuhu, when the sight reaches it.

The Exalted said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, meaning the lawful things. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾. Righteousness (ṣalāḥ) is steadfastness upon what the Shari'ah (the revealed law) requires. ﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾.

The rest read it with a shaddah on the nun, as "in the sense of" (ʿalā maʿnā) "and that this" [32a]. ﴿We hasten to them with good things﴾, i.e., We make for them good things, and We advance them as a reward for their deeds, as a sign of Our approval of them. ﴿Nay, but they do not perceive﴾ that this is a gradual drawing-on (istidraj) for them.

Al-ishfaq (apprehension) is fear, and the meaning is that the believers, by reason of the fear of God that they have, are fearful of His punishment. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "The believer is one who combines good deeds with fear, and the hypocrite is one who combines evil deeds with feeling secure." [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 18/32.]]

﴿And those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾, i.e., they affirm them.

﴿And those who do not associate anything with their Lord﴾.

﴿And those who give what they give﴾, i.e., they give what they have been given of zakat and charities. It is narrated from Aisha that she used to recite "wa-alladhina ya'tuna ma ataw" (those who come with what they came with), i.e., they do the acts of righteousness that they have done. ﴿And their hearts are trembling﴾ lest that does not save them from the punishment of God, and lest their deeds are not accepted from them, ﴿that they are returning to their Lord﴾, because they are certain that they will return to God, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Hasan said: "They worked for God through acts of obedience [and exerted themselves in them] [[The text within the brackets is absent from manuscript "a".]] and feared that they would be rejected."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 23, verses 61–64:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Those hasten towards the good deeds, and they are foremost in them.﴾ They hasten to righteous deeds. ﴿And they are foremost in them﴾ means: they are foremost towards them, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for what they were forbidden﴾, meaning "towards what they were forbidden", and "for what they said" and similar expressions. Ibn 'Abbas said regarding the meaning of this verse: happiness (al-sa'adah) preceded for them from Allah. Al-Kalbi said: they outstripped the nations in good deeds.

His saying: ﴿And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾ means: beyond its ability (tawqah). Whoever is unable to stand, let him pray seated; and whoever is unable to fast, let him break his fast.

﴿And with Us is a Book which speaks with the truth﴾ This is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). "Speaks with the truth" means it makes clear with honesty. The meaning of the verse is: Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity, except what it is able to do of deeds, and We have recorded its deeds in the Preserved Tablet, so it speaks of them and makes them clear. It was also said: it is the recording of the deeds of the servants which the recording angels (al-hafazah) write down. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, neither will any of their good deeds be diminished, nor will anything be added to their evil deeds.

Then He mentioned the disbelievers, saying: ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion﴾ meaning: in heedlessness and ignorance, ﴿concerning this﴾ meaning: concerning the Qur'an, ﴿and they have deeds other than that﴾ meaning: the disbelievers have wicked deeds of sins and transgressions, decreed against them, other than that, meaning other than the deeds of the believers which Allah mentioned in His saying: "Indeed, those who are apprehensive out of fear of their Lord" ﴿they are doers of them﴾. They must perform them, and thereby enter the Fire, because of the misery that preceded for them. This is the saying of most of the exegetes. Qatadah said: this refers to the Muslims, and that they have deeds besides the good deeds they have done, which they are doing; but the first view is more evident.

﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾ meaning: We seize their wealthy and their leaders. ﴿With punishment﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the sword on the day of Badr. Al-Dahhak said: it means hunger, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, saying: "O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make for them years like the years of Joseph" [[A fragment of a hadith narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Supplications, chapter on supplicating against the polytheists with defeat and earthquake: 11/193–194, and by Muslim in the Book of Mosques, chapter: the recommendation of qunut in all prayers, no. (675), 1/466–467.]] So Allah afflicted them with drought, until they ate dogs and carrion.

﴿Behold, they cry out for help﴾ meaning: they cry out, lament, and plead for help. The origin of al-ja'r (crying out) is raising the voice in supplication.

**Qur'anic verse 65:** "Do not cry out for help today; indeed you will not be helped by Us."

That is, do not wail (lā taj'arū: do not cry out). "Indeed you will not be helped by Us": you will not be protected from Us, and your supplication will not benefit you.

**Verse 66:** "My verses were recited to you, but you turned back on your heels."

"My verses" means the Qur'an. "You turned back on your heels" means you drew back backward, recoiling from faith.

**Verse 67:** "Arrogant about it, speaking nonsense by night, [and] talking of it."

Scholars differed over the pronoun in "about it" (bihi). The most apparent view is that it refers to the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Ḥarām), as an implicit reference not previously mentioned. That is: arrogant, magnifying themselves through the Sacred House. Their self-magnification through it was that they would say, "We are the people of God's Sanctuary and the neighbours of His House; no one will overpower us, and we fear no one," so they felt secure within it while all other people were in fear. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and a group. It was also said that "about it" means about the Qur'an, so they did not believe in it. The first view is more apparent: what is meant is the Sanctuary.

"Sāmiran" (talking together by night, as a companion in conversation) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning that they would converse at night in their gatherings around the House. The singular "sāmiran" is used although its sense is plural (al-summār, the evening talkers), because it was placed in the position of a time expression; the meaning is "you used to shun [the Qur'an] at night." It was also said: the singular is used while the meaning is plural, as in His saying, "Then We bring you out as infants" (Qur'an 22:5).

"Tahjurūn" (you talk nonsense): Nafi' read "tuhjirūn" with a dammah on the first letter and a kasrah on the jim, from al-ihjār, which is indecent speech; that is, you utter obscenities and say foul things. It is mentioned that they used to revile the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions. The others read "tahjurūn" with a fatḥah on the first letter and a ḍammah on the jim, meaning you turn away from the Prophet (ﷺ), from faith, and from the Qur'an, and reject them. It was also said: it is from al-hajr, meaning foul speech; one says hajara yahjuru hajran when he speaks what is not true. It was also said: it means you mock and say what you do not know, from their saying: "The man spoke nonsense (hajara) in his sleep" when he raved.

**Verse 68:** "Have they not then pondered the Word, or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?"

That is, "yadabbarū" means "yatadabbarū" (they reflect). "The Word" means what came to them of speech, which is the Qur'an, so that they would recognise in it the proofs of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ). "Or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?" So they denied it. The meaning is: We have sent messengers before them to their peoples, and in the same way We have sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to them. It was also said: "am" (or) here means "bal" (rather), meaning: there has come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old, and therefore they denied it.

**Verse 69:** "Or have they not recognised their Messenger, so that they deny him?"

Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas said: Did they not know Muhammad (ﷺ) as a youth and as an adult? They knew his lineage, his truthfulness, his trustworthiness, and his fulfilment of covenants. This is said as a rebuke to them for turning away from him after they had recognised him for truthfulness and trustworthiness.

That is, do not wail (lā taj'arū: do not cry out). "Indeed you will not be helped by Us": you will not be protected from Us, and your supplication will not benefit you.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 23, verses 70–74:**

﴿Or do they say, "There is madness in him"?﴾ Madness (*junun*). But it is not so. ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth,﴾ meaning with sincerity and with a word whose soundness and excellence are not hidden from any person of intellect. ﴿But most of them are averse to the truth.﴾

﴿And if the truth had followed their desires...﴾ Ibn Jurayj, Muqatil, al-Suddi, and a group of scholars said: "The truth" here is Allah, meaning: if Allah had followed their wishes in what He does. It was also said: if He had followed their desires, He would have named for Himself a partner and a son, as they say. ﴿...the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted.﴾ Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the intended meaning of "the truth" is the Qur'an, meaning: if the Qur'an had come with what they love, such as the making of partners and offspring for Allah, according to what they believe, ﴿the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted, and whoever is in them.﴾ This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If there had been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22].

﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾ meaning, that which reminds them. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning that in which lies their pride and their honour, namely the Qur'an. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 10], meaning your honour, and ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44], meaning an honour for you and your people.

﴿Yet they are, from their reminder, turning away﴾ meaning, from their honour. ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment?﴾ in return for what you have brought them, ﴿kharjan﴾, meaning a wage or reward. ﴿But the payment of your Lord is better,﴾ meaning what Allah gives you of His provision and reward is better, ﴿and He is the best of providers.﴾

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *kharajan* and *fakharaju* both with an alif (ألف), while Ibn 'Amir read both without an alif. The rest read *kharjan* without an alif and *fakharaju* with an alif.

﴿And indeed, you invite them to a straight path,﴾ which is Islam.

﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path,﴾ meaning from the religion of truth, ﴿deviating﴾ meaning inclining away and swerving.

﴿وَلَوْ رَحِمْنَاهُمْ وَكَشَفْنَا مَا بِهِمْ مِنْ ضُرٍّ﴾ "Even if We had shown them mercy and removed the harm that is upon them," meaning drought and famine, ﴿لَلَجُّوا﴾ "they would persist," meaning they would keep on, ﴿فِي طُغْيَانِهِمْ يَعْمَهُونَ﴾ "in their rebellion, wandering blindly." And they would not be restrained from it.

﴿وَلَقَدْ أَخَذْنَاهُمْ بِالْعَذَابِ﴾ "We had already seized them with punishment." The reason is that the Prophet (ﷺ) invoked against the Quraysh that God would send upon them years like the years of Joseph. Famine struck them, and Abu Sufyan came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "I implore you by God and by the ties of kinship. Do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?" He said: "Yes." He said: "You have killed the fathers with the sword and the sons with hunger, so pray to God that He lift this famine from us." He prayed, and it was lifted from them. Then God revealed this verse. [[See al-Tabari: 18/45; Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, pp. 362–363; al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/111; al-Sahih al-Musnad min Asbab al-Nuzul by Shaykh Muqbil ibn Hadi, p. 100.]] ﴿فَمَا اسْتَكَانُوا لِرَبِّهِمْ﴾ "But they did not humble themselves before their Lord." That is, they did not submit and did not become humble before their Lord. Its root meaning is seeking tranquility (sukun). ﴿وَمَا يَتَضَرَّعُونَ﴾ "Nor did they plead," that is, they did not supplicate humbly to their Lord, but persisted in their defiance.

﴿حَتَّى إِذَا فَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ بَابًا ذَا عَذَابٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾ "Until, when We opened upon them a gate of severe punishment." Ibn Abbas said: it means the killing on the day of Badr. Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 81–88:

﴿Nay, but they said the like of what the ancients said.﴾ That is: they denied just as the ancients denied.

﴿They said: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised up?"﴾ (lamab'uthun) meaning: shall we indeed be gathered (lamahshurun). They said this by way of denial and astonishment.

﴿Indeed we and our fathers were promised this before,﴾ the promise, ﴿before﴾ meaning: a people who claimed to be messengers of God promised our fathers, but we have seen no reality of it. ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ (asatir al-awwalin), that is, the lies of the ancients.

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, answering them, meaning the people of Makkah, ﴿"To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it of creation, if you know?"﴾ meaning: who is its Creator and its Owner.

﴿They will say, "To God."﴾ And they must say this, because they acknowledge that it is created.

﴿Say﴾ to them, when they have acknowledged that: ﴿"Then will you not remember?"﴾ so that you would know that the One who was able to create the earth and whoever is in it at the beginning is able to revive them after death.

﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?"﴾

﴿They will say, "God."﴾ The majority of readers recite "lillah" (to God), and likewise what follows it, so they made the answer according to the meaning, like the saying of one who asks a man, "Who is your patron?" and he replies, "To so-and-so," meaning: I belong to so-and-so, and he is my patron. The people of Basra recite "Allah" in both places, and it is so in the Basran codex, while in the other codices it is written with an alif like the first. ﴿Say: "Will you then not fear God?"﴾ that is, be wary.

﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of everything?"﴾ Malakut means kingship (al-mulk), and the ta' in it is for emphasis (al-mubalaghah). ﴿And He protects,﴾ that is, He grants security to whom He wills, ﴿while none can be protected against Him,﴾ that is, none can grant security to one whom God wills to frighten, or He protects whom He wills from evil, and none can protect from Him one whom He intends with evil. ﴿If you know﴾ — it is said: its meaning is, "Answer, if you know."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 89–96:

﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say, "Then how are you deluded?"﴾ That is: you are deceived and turned away from His oneness and obedience. The meaning is: how is the truth made to appear to you as falsehood?

﴿Rather, We have brought them the truth﴾, with sincerity, ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾ in what they claim of a partner, ٣٣/أ [33a] ﴿Allah has not taken any offspring, and there is not with Him any god. Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾. That is: no partner. ﴿Each god would have taken away what he created﴾: that is, each would have been singled out with what he created, and would not have been content for his creation and bounty to be attributed to another, and he would have prevented the other god from seizing what he created.

﴿And some of them would have overcome others﴾: that is, some would have sought to overpower others, like the kings of this world among themselves. Then He declared Himself free of imperfection, saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾. ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. The people of Madina and Kufa, except Hafs, read "عَالِمُ" (ʿālimu) with a raised mim, as a beginning (nominative), while the others read it with a lowered mim (ʿālimi), as an epithet of Allah in "سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ" (Subhana Llah). ﴿So exalted is He above what they associate﴾: that is, He is magnified above what they associate; its meaning is that He is far greater than to be described by this description.

His saying: ﴿Say, "My Lord, if You should show me﴾: that is, if You show me, ﴿what they are promised﴾: that is, what You have promised them of punishment.

﴿My Lord﴾: that is, O my Lord, ﴿then do not place me among the wrongdoing people﴾: that is, do not destroy me along with their destruction.

﴿And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them﴾ of punishment, ﴿[indeed, We are Able]﴾.

﴿Repel evil with that which is best﴾: that is, repel with the best manner, which is forgiveness, turning away, and patience, ﴿the evil﴾, meaning their harm. He commanded them to be patient with the harm of the polytheists and to refrain from fighting. It was abrogated (nasakhat) by the verse of the sword. [[It has been mentioned in more than one place that the scholars extended the abrogation of many verses of patience, forgiveness and gentle dealing by the verse of the sword, while the truth is that there is no abrogation in this. See what has preceded: 3/32–33.]] ﴿We are most knowing of what they describe﴾: they lie and say of shirk.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 23, verses 97–101:**

﴿Say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You"﴾, meaning: I refrain and take refuge in You, ﴿from the whispers (hamazat) of the devils﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "Their incitements (nazarat)." Al-Hasan said: "Their whisperings (waswasa)." Mujahid said: "Their breathing and their spitting." The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: "Their pushing (daf'uhum) into sins through seduction. The root of hamz is intense pushing."

﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, from their presence (yahdurun) with me﴾ in any of my affairs. He mentioned presence because when the devil is present, he whispers to a person. Then He informed that these disbelievers, who deny the Resurrection, ask to be returned to the world at the moment of witnessing death. So He said: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: "My Lord, send me back"﴾. He did not say "send me back" (irji'ni) but "send us back" (irji'unі), while he is asking Allah alone for the return. This follows the custom of the Arabs, who address one person with the plural form out of respect, as Allah the Exalted related about Himself: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]. Similar usages are numerous in the Qur'an. It was also said: this address is to the angels who take his soul, beginning with an address to Allah, because they first called upon Allah for help and then turned to asking the angels for a return to the world.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿So that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind﴾, meaning: what I neglected, namely saying "There is no god but Allah." It was also said: that I may act in obedience to Allah. Qatadah said: He did not wish to return to his family and clan, nor to gather worldly wealth and fulfil desires, but he wished to return and act in obedience to Allah. May Allah have mercy on the one who acts in what the disbeliever wishes for when he sees the punishment.

﴿No!﴾ is a word of repulsion and rebuke, meaning: he will not return. ﴿Indeed, it is only a word he is saying﴾, referring to his request for return. ﴿And behind them is a barzakh (barrier) until the Day they are resurrected﴾. Barzakh means a partition between two things. Its meaning here is disputed. Mujahid said: "A barrier between them and returning to the world." Qatadah said: "The remainder of the world." Al-Dahhak said: "The barzakh is what lies between death and resurrection." It was also said: it is the grave, and they remain in it until the Day they are resurrected.

﴿Then when the Horn is blown, there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask about one another﴾. The scholars differed concerning this blast. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that it is the first blast: ﴿And the Horn is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth falls unconscious﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]; ﴿so there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask about one another﴾; then ﴿He blows it again, and at once they are standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]; ﴿and they turn to one another, questioning﴾ [al-Saffat: 27].

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that it is the second blast. He said: On the Day of Resurrection the male and female servant will be taken by the hand and set up before the first and last generations. Then a caller will call out: "This is so-and-so, son of so-and-so. Whoever has a right against him, let him come and take his right." A man will rejoice if the right is owed to him by his father, his child, his wife or his brother, so he takes from him. Then Ibn Mas'ud recited: "So there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask about one another." [Al-Tabari narrated both reports: 18/54.]

In the narration of Ata from Ibn Abbas: it is the second blast. "So there will be no kinship between them" means they will not boast of lineages that Day as they used to boast in the world, and "they will not ask about one another" in the manner of seeking connection, as they used to ask in the world: "Who are you, and from which tribe are you?" It is not meant that lineages will be severed.

If it is objected: Has it not come in a hadith: "Every cause and every lineage will be cut off except my lineage and my cause"? [A portion of a hadith narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak: 3/142, from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "This hadith has a sound chain but they did not record it." al-Dhahabi said: "It is discontinuous (munqati')." Al-Tabarani: 3/37; al-Haythami, 4/272, said: "Al-Tabarani narrated it and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih." Al-Bayhaqi: 7/114. Ibn Hajar mentioned it in al-Matalib al-Aliya: 4/177 and attributed it to Ibn Abi Umar. Al-Busiri said: "Its narrators are trustworthy." al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/117 to al-Bazzar and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara. See also Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/257.]

It is answered: its meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection no cause and no lineage will remain beneficial except his lineage and his cause, which are faith and the Qur'an.

If it is objected: Here He said ﴿nor will they ask about one another﴾, and in another place He said: "And they turn to one another, questioning" [al-Saffat: 27].

The answer: what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that the Resurrection has states and stations. In one station, fear will be intense upon them, and the magnitude of the matter will preoccupy them from questioning, so they do not ask one another. In another station they will recover consciousness and so they will ask one another. [See the Questions of al-Razi and their Answers, p. 238.]

It was also said: that I may act in obedience to Allah. Al-Dahhak said: "The barzakh is what lies between death and resurrection." It was also said: it is the grave, and they remain in it until the Day they are resurrected.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 109–111:**

﴿Indeed, it﴾. The *ha'* in *innahu* is an *ʿimād* (a dummy or separator pronoun, sometimes called *al-majhūla*, "the unknown one"). ﴿There was a group of My servants﴾, who are the believers, ﴿who said: "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful"﴾. ﴿But you took them in mockery﴾. Ahl al-Madina, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *sukhriyyan* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* here and in Surah Sad, while the rest read it with a *kasra*. All agreed on the *ḍamma* in Surah al-Zukhruf. Al-Khalil said: "Both are dialectal variants, like their saying *baḥrun lujjiyyun* and *lijjiyyun* (with *ḍamma* and *kasra* on the *lām*), and *kawkabun durriyyun* and *durriyyun*." Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: "The *kasra* means mockery in speech, and the *ḍamma* means subjugation and enslavement in action." They agreed that in Surah al-Zukhruf it means subjugation. ﴿Until they made you forget My remembrance﴾, meaning: your preoccupation with mocking them and subjugating them made you forget My remembrance. ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾. A parallel is the verse: "Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed" [al-Mutaffifin: 29]. Muqatil said: "It was revealed concerning Bilal, Ammar, Khabbab, Suhayb, Salman and the poor among the Companions, whom the disbelievers of Quraysh used to mock." [See al-Bahr al-Muhit: 6/423.]

﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for their patience﴾, for their patience under your harm and your mockery in the world. ﴿That they are the triumphant ones﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *annahum* with a *kasra* on the *alif*, as a new sentence (*istiʾnāf*). The others read it with a *fatḥa*, so it occupies the position of the second object: "I have rewarded them today, for their patience, with the triumph of Paradise."

He said, "How many years did you remain on the earth?" [23:112]

Hamza and al-Kisa'i (two of the seven canonical readers) read *"Qul kam labithtum"* ("Say: How many years did you remain?") in the imperative. The meaning of the verse is: "Say, O disbelievers." The address is given in the singular form, while what is meant is the group, since the meaning is understood. It is also possible that the address is to each one of them individually, meaning: "Say, O disbelievers." Ibn Kathir read *"Qul kam"* in the imperative, but read *"Qala inna"* ("He said, verily") in the indicative, because the second is an answer. The rest of the readers read *"Qala"* ("He said") in both places, meaning: God, Mighty and Majestic, said to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, "How many years did you remain?" ﴿on the earth﴾, that is, in the world and in the graves, ﴿counting years﴾.

They said, ﴿"We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who keep count."﴾ They forgot the length of their stay in the world because of the magnitude of the punishment they were facing. ﴿Those who keep count﴾ are the angels who guard the deeds of the children of Adam and record them against them.

He said, ﴿"You remained only a little"﴾, that is, what you remained in the world. He called it "little" because, however long a person's stay in the world may be, it is little compared with what he remains in the Hereafter, since his stay in the world and in the grave is finite. ﴿If only you had known﴾ the measure of your stay in the world.

The words of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿"Did you think that We created you in vain"﴾, meaning in play and falsehood, without wisdom. The word *"'abathan"* ("in vain") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: playing. It has also been said that it means "for play," that is, "that you might play and sport, just as We created the beasts, which have no reward and no punishment." This is like His words: "Does man think that he will be left neglected?" [75:36]. Rather, you were created for worship and for the establishment of God's commands, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿"And that you would not be returned to Us"﴾, that is: Did you think that you would not be returned to Us in the Hereafter for recompense? Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read *"la turja'un"* ("you will not be returned") with a fatha on the *ta'* and a kasra on the *jim*, in the active form.

Abd al-Wahid al-Malihi related to us; Abu Mansur Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Sam'an related to us; Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-Rayyani related to us; Humayd ibn Zanjawayh related to us; Bishr ibn Umar related to us; Abdullah ibn Lahi'a related to us; Abdullah ibn Hubayra related to us, from Hansh, that a man afflicted (with illness) was brought past Ibn Mas'ud, and he recited over his ears ﴿"Did you think that We created you in vain"﴾ until he finished the surah, and he was healed. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "With what did you recite over his ear?" So he informed him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, if a man with certainty recited it over a mountain, it would move."[[Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr (6/122) as narrated by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Sunni in 'Amal al-Yawm wal-Layla (p. 298), Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya (1/7), and Ibn Mardawayh. In its chain is Salam ibn Razin, who is unknown, and his hadith is false. Al-Dhahabi mentioned it in al-Mizan (2/175) and said: al-Uqayli said: Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal related to us, saying... and he related the hadith. My father said: This is fabricated; this is the hadith of liars.]]

So he informed him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, if a man with certainty recited it over a mountain, it would move."[[Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr (6/122) as narrated by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Sunni in 'Amal al-Yawm wal-Layla (p. 298), Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya (1/7), and Ibn Mardawayh. He said, "How many years did you remain on the earth?" [23:112]

Hamza and al-Kisa'i (two of the seven canonical readers) read *"Qul kam labithtum"* ("Say: How many years did you remain?") in the imperative. The meaning of the verse is: "Say, O disbelievers." The address is given in the singular form, while what is meant is the group, since the meaning is understood. It is also possible that the address is to each one of them individually, meaning: "Say, O disbelievers." Ibn Kathir read *"Qul kam"* in the imperative, but read *"Qala inna"* ("He said, verily") in the indicative, because the second is an answer. The rest of the readers read *"Qala"* ("He said") in both places, meaning: God, Mighty and Majestic, said to the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, "How many years did you remain?" ﴿on the earth﴾, that is, in the world and in the graves, ﴿counting years﴾.

They said, ﴿"We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who keep count."﴾ They forgot the length of their stay in the world because of the magnitude of the punishment they were facing. ﴿Those who keep count﴾ are the angels who guard the deeds of the children of Adam and record them against them.

He said, ﴿"You remained only a little"﴾, that is, what you remained in the world. He called it "little" because, however long a person's stay in the world may be, it is little compared with what he remains in the Hereafter, since his stay in the world and in the grave is finite. ﴿If only you had known﴾ the measure of your stay in the world.

The words of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿"Did you think that We created you in vain"﴾, meaning in play and falsehood, without wisdom. The word *"'abathan"* ("in vain") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning: playing. It has also been said that it means "for play," that is, "that you might play and sport, just as We created the beasts, which have no reward and no punishment." This is like His words: "Does man think that he will be left neglected?" [75:36]. Rather, you were created for worship and for the establishment of God's commands, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿"And that you would not be returned to Us"﴾, that is: Did you think that you would not be returned to Us in the Hereafter for recompense? Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read *"la turja'un"* ("you will not be returned") with a fatha on the *ta'* and a kasra on the *jim*, in the active form.

Then Allah declared Himself free of what the polytheists attribute to Him, so He said, mighty is His remembrance: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth. There is no deity except Him, Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾ "The Noble Throne" means the beautiful throne. It is also said: the elevated one.

﴿And whoever calls upon another deity besides Allah, for which he has no proof﴾ meaning: he has no argument for it and no evidence, because there is no argument for the claim of associating partners with Allah. ﴿Then his account is with his Lord﴾ meaning his recompense: He will repay him for his deeds, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed, upon Us is their account﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 26]. ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾ meaning: whoever denies and disbelieves will not attain felicity.

﴿And say, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾
